hints: Think about what the white ionic product must be when $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ meets water and hydroxide ions form.
walkthrough:
Work out the second product**
You are told ethyne, $\mathrm{C_2H_2}$, forms plus a sparingly soluble white ionic compound. Calcium compounds that are white and sparingly soluble point straight to calcium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$. The carbide ion $\mathrm{C_2^{2-}}$ picks up two $\mathrm{H^+}$ from two waters to make $\mathrm{C_2H_2}$, leaving $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ with two $\mathrm{OH^-}$.

Balance the atoms**
One $\mathrm{CaC_2}$ needs two $\mathrm{H_2O}$ to supply two H for ethyne and two OH for $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$. That gives $$\mathrm{CaC_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow C_2H_2 + Ca(OH)_2}$$ which is balanced for Ca, C, H and O.

hints: Count outer electrons for $\mathrm{C_2^{2-}}$: each C brings 4 valence electrons plus 2 extra for the 2- charge, then think how many must be shared to give each C an octet.
walkthrough:
Count the electrons to show**
Each carbon has 4 outer electrons, so two carbons give 8, plus 2 more for the 2- charge gives 10 electrons total. That is 5 pairs to place.

Share three pairs for the triple bond**
Like in $\mathrm{N_2}$, each C needs an octet. Put three shared pairs between the two C atoms in the overlap region, using dots for one C and crosses for the other. Then place one lone pair (two dots or two crosses) on the outside of each C. Enclose in brackets with a 2- charge.
Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram of $\mathrm{[:C \equiv C:]^{2-}}$ showing a triple bond (3 shared pairs) plus one lone pair on each C; outer electrons only, with 2- charge shown.

hints: Compare $\mathrm{C_2H_2}$, $\mathrm{C_3H_4}$ and $\mathrm{C_4H_6}$ and look at how H changes as C increases by one.
walkthrough:
Spot the pattern**
Ethyne is $\mathrm{C_2H_2}$, propyne is $\mathrm{C_3H_4}$, butyne is $\mathrm{C_4H_6}$. Each time C goes up by 1, H goes up by 2. For $n$ carbons, H is $2n-2$. Check: $n=2$ gives $\mathrm{C_2H_2}$. So the general formula is $$\mathrm{C_nH_{2n-2}}$$

hints: Look at the repeat unit of poly(acetylene): every carbon is part of a C=C double bond in a long chain, so think where mobile charge carriers could come from.
walkthrough:
See the long chain of pi bonds**
The structure shows alternating double and single bonds all along the chain. Each C=C has pi electrons. Because the double bonds are conjugated, the p orbitals overlap along the whole chain.

Link mobility to conduction**
That overlap lets pi electrons become delocalised and move along the chain when a voltage is applied, just like delocalised electrons in a metal or graphite. Mobile charged particles mean electrical conduction.
Final answer: Contains delocalised electrons that are mobile along the polymer chain and can carry charge.

hints: Read the atoms in one repeat unit $\mathrm{CH=CH}$ and simplify to the lowest whole number ratio.
walkthrough:
Simplify the repeat unit**
One repeat unit shown is $\mathrm{C_2H_2}$. Empirical means simplest ratio, so divide by 2 to get $\mathrm{CH}$.

hints: Think about a physical property like mass per volume, or a chemical property like rusting, where a plastic is very different from iron or copper.
walkthrough:
Compare plastic to metal**
Polymers are made of light C and H atoms with relatively open packing, so they are much less dense than metals. They also do not corrode like metals and are flexible and can be moulded. Any one valid physical or chemical advantage is enough, for example lower density.
Final answer: Less dense (lighter) than metals / does not corrode / more flexible.

hints: Identify the nucleophile and electrophile: the $\mathrm{R-C \equiv C^-}$ has a lone pair, the carbonyl C is electron poor.
Recall how to show a carbonyl dipole and where a curly arrow must start and finish for attack on C=O.
Think about what charge ends up on oxygen after the pi bond breaks and how the new C-C bond looks in the intermediate.
walkthrough:
Mark the carbonyl dipole**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the carbonyl is polarised $\mathrm{C^{\delta+}-O^{\delta-}}$. Label $\delta^+$ on C and $\delta^-$ on O. That $\delta^+$ carbon is the electrophile.

Draw the attack arrow**
The acetylide ion $\mathrm{R-C \equiv C^-}$ has a lone pair on carbon. Draw a curly arrow starting at that lone pair and pointing to the $\delta^+$ carbonyl carbon to form the new C-C bond. At the same time draw a second curly arrow from the $\mathrm{C=O}$ double bond up onto O, because the pi bond breaks heterolytically.

Write the alkoxide intermediate**
Joining the fragments gives $\mathrm{R-C \equiv C-C(R')(R'')-O^-}$. Carbon now has four single bonds, oxygen carries the negative charge as an alkoxide. This is later protonated to the alcohol shown in reaction 1.

Final answer: Curly arrow from lone pair on $\mathrm{R-C \equiv C^-}$ to carbonyl C ($\delta^+$); curly arrow from $\mathrm{C=O}$ bond to O; $\delta^+$ on C and $\delta^-$ on O of $\mathrm{R'-C(=O)-R''}$; intermediate $\mathrm{R-C \equiv C-C(R')(R'')-O^-}$.

hints: A negatively charged carbon joining to a carbonyl C followed by protonation to an alcohol is the classic addition pattern for carbonyls.
walkthrough:
Name the pattern**
A nucleophile ($\mathrm{R-C \equiv C^-}$) adds to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon and the C=O is converted to C-O. No atoms are lost or substituted, the reagent simply adds across the double bond. That is nucleophilic addition.
Final answer: Nucleophilic addition

hints: Split product P at each new $\mathrm{C-C(OH)}$ bond: the $\mathrm{C_2H_5-C \equiv C-}$ fragment must come from the alkyne, the rest of the central carbon skeleton from the carbonyl.
Notice P is symmetrical with two identical alkyne additions, so count how many Q molecules reacted and work out what dicarbonyl R must have two C=O groups that both became $\mathrm{C-OH}$.
walkthrough:
Pull out the alkyne fragment**
In reaction 1, the group $\mathrm{R-C \equiv C-}$ in the product comes unchanged from $\mathrm{R-C \equiv C-H}$. In P you see two identical $\mathrm{C_2H_5-C \equiv C-}$ groups attached to C-OH carbons. So Q must be $\mathrm{C_2H_5-C \equiv C-H}$, which is but-1-yne. It must be terminal (has C-H) to form the anion.

Rebuild the carbonyl compound**
Each $\mathrm{C-OH}$ in P was a $\mathrm{C=O}$ in R. Removing the two alkyne parts and converting both $\mathrm{C(OH)(CH_3)-}$ units back to $\mathrm{C(=O)(CH_3)-}$ leaves $\mathrm{CH_3-C(=O)-CH_2-C(=O)-CH_3}$. That is pentane-2,4-dione. Two moles of Q add to one mole of this diketone to give P.
Final answer: Q: $\mathrm{C_2H_5-C \equiv C-H}$ (but-1-yne); R: $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2COCH_3}$ (pentane-2,4-dione).

hints: Recall which functional groups decolourise hot acidified $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$: aldehydes and carboxylic acids with oxidisable groups do, simple ketones resist.
Recall the iodoform rule: only molecules with $\mathrm{CH_3CO-}$ or $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)-}$ give a yellow precipitate with alkaline $\mathrm{I_2}$.
Recall Tollens rule: only aldehydes (and formic acid which contains an aldehyde-like H-C=O unit) give the silver mirror.
Apply the three rules to ethanedioic acid $\mathrm{HO_2CCO_2H}$: it is a strong reducing agent for manganate but has no methyl ketone and no aldehyde group.
walkthrough:
Sort the manganate oxidations**
Hot acidified $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ is a powerful oxidiser. $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$ is oxidised to ethanoic acid, tick. $\mathrm{HCO_2H}$ (formic acid) is oxidised to $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and water, tick. $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$ has no H on the carbonyl and resists, cross. $\mathrm{HO_2CCO_2H}$ (ethanedioic acid) is famously oxidised to $\mathrm{CO_2}$, tick.

Sort the iodoform tests**
Alkaline $\mathrm{I_2}$ gives yellow $\mathrm{CHI_3}$ only with $\mathrm{CH_3CO-}$ groups. $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$ can form this grouping, tick. $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$ is the classic positive, tick. $\mathrm{HCO_2H}$ and $\mathrm{HO_2CCO_2H}$ have no methyl ketone unit, both cross.

Sort Tollens reagent**
Tollens oxidises aldehydes to carboxylates giving a silver mirror. $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$ is an aldehyde, tick. $\mathrm{HCO_2H}$ contains $\mathrm{H-C(=O)-}$ and also reduces Tollens, tick. $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$ is a ketone, cross. $\mathrm{HO_2CCO_2H}$ has only carboxylic acid groups, cross.

Assemble the table**
Row 1 (manganate): tick, tick, cross, tick. Row 2 (iodoform): tick, cross, tick, cross. Row 3 (Tollens): tick, tick, cross, cross. This pattern uniquely distinguishes all four compounds.

Final answer: hot acidified $\mathrm{MnO_4^-(aq)}$: $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$ tick, $\mathrm{HCO_2H}$ tick, $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$ cross, $\mathrm{HO_2CCO_2H}$ tick; alkaline $\mathrm{I_2(aq)}$: $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$ tick, $\mathrm{HCO_2H}$ cross, $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$ tick, $\mathrm{HO_2CCO_2H}$ cross; warm Tollens: $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$ tick, $\mathrm{HCO_2H}$ tick, $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$ cross, $\mathrm{HO_2CCO_2H}$ cross.
